Split-screen

You might say

Split the home page in half—brand intro on the left, login on the right—and stack them on phones.

Give two parallel tasks two near-equal halves of one view·Login pages often put the brand story on the left half and the form on the right; entry pages can give personal and enterprise plans one half each. It only counts as split-screen when both sides truly run parallel tasks; on phones a side-by-side split is unreadable, so stack the areas and decide yourself which one comes first.

Two halves · parallel tasks

You can say this to an AI Agent

“

Make the login page a split-screen: the left half carries the brand intro with a “Learn more” entry, the right half carries the login form; both sides are parallel tasks with similar visual weight. On phones, stack them vertically with the form first. Then check on desktop and mobile: does each side read as its own task, and are inputs and buttons usable on the phone.

Split-screen≠Sidebar

In Sidebar the sidebar is navigation with clearly less weight than the workspace; in Split-screen both sides carry near-equal, independent tasks.

Split-screen≠Image plus text

In an image-plus-text row the image only serves the text; in Split-screen each side carries its own task or entry, and removing either one loses a real job.

When to use it

  • Login and signup pages: brand story on one side, the form on the other
    Brand introLogin form
  • Two audience entries: personal vs business, buyer vs seller
    PersonalBusiness
  • Two product paths: start a trial vs book a demo
    Start a trialBook a demo
  • Two plans or versions compared side by side at similar weight
    Plan A · annual billingPlan B · monthly billing

When NOT to use it

  • One side is only a decorative image while the other holds the only task
    All content sits on the right
  • A wide content area with a narrow sidebar is a sidebar layout instead
  • Keeping the side-by-side split on phones until text and buttons shrink
  • Cramming both halves full until the first screen becomes two crowded pages

Each side has its own headline and action, unlike a decorative image-plus-text pair
